subject: Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
Hi folks,

I'm making progress in my learning of both bayesian methods and using stan itself. However, I've encountered a phenomenon that I don't quite understand. To check my understanding of things, I've implemented what I think is code to generate data from a hierarchical Gaussian model (one random effect & one 2-level fixed effect) then evaluate credible values of the data-generating parameters using rstan (i.e. pretending I didn't generate the data with known parameter values). Here's the code:

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/4989099

However, I find that even when I run chains of 10,000 iterations (takes about 1hr on my system), I'm still getting strong autocorrelation in some of the parameters. Here's a link to a dropbox folder where I've put the .RData files for each chain and the ggmcmc output:

https://www.dropbox.com/sh/velltjr8qyih3nh/wQ60qqsZbo

Any suggestions on what I've done wrong?

Mike

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
Mike,

This might be due to a known "feature" of HMC, where the variation in the potential energy in a trajectory is limited to about (number of dimensions) / 2.  In hierarchical models, however, the variation within the bulk of the probability mass can be much larger than d / 2 and so no matter how long you run a single trajectory you'll never rid yourself of autocorrelation.  See, for example, the discussion in http://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4693.  

Of course it might also have to do with poor adaptation due to widely differing parameter scales.  Have you tried standardizing your data?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
On Wednesday, February 20, 2013 9:40:54 AM UTC-5, Mike Lawrence wrote:
Any suggestions on what I've done wrong?

Nothing really jumped out at me from a quick glance at your code. But, for large samples, this

// now go through the data and calculate the log-probability of each data point (summing as you go to eventually get the sum log probability)
for(i in 1:L){
  lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log( y[i] , n_mu[unit[i],condition[i]] , sigma );
}

can be unnecessarily slow in wall time, although it has nothing to do with the autocorrelation. Better to declare a local variable like mu_temp, fill it with a loop, and then do the likelihood. Like

for(i in 1:L) {
  mu_temp[i] <- n_mu[unit[i],condition[i]];
}
y ~ normal(mu_temp, sigma);

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
For what it's worth, the implicit uniform prior on correlation
matrices is proper. The set of correlation matrices
forms a compact space in R^N because correlations are
bounded between -1 and 1. The same things happens in
providing a proper uniform prior for real variables declared
with lower and upper bounds and for simplexes, which bound
values between 0 and 1.

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
One should be careful when computing anything that's not an
expectation with correlated samples, since those estimates may be
biased. An easy fix is to thin the samples until they are nearly
uncorrelated. But you should always be cautious—estimates of 95%
intervals are very noisy under the best of circumstances, since by
definition almost all of the samples tell you almost nothing about
where exactly the 95% interval is.

One should of course also be careful when computing things that _are_
expectations as well, if the sample looks unreliable.

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
95% intervals are harder to estimate than means (i.e., you
need more effective samples because only the bottom 2.5% and
top 2.5% of samples are relevant for a central 95% interval).

If you have converged and have enough effective samples, then
yes, you should be OK.

I'm not sure how much we should trust lower level parameters in
a hierarchical model if the hierarchical parameters have low
numbers of effective samples. Maybe someone else on the list
will know.

- Bob

A "proper" density integrates to 1 over the
parameters. For instance, a uniform on (-inf,inf)
or on (0,inf) isn't proper because the integral
diverges.

- Bob

messages.author: 6e0bce06355e4e6c
messages.subject: Re: Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
Hi Bob,

BUGS approximates the effective sample size in terms of MCMC error; the rule of thumb is usually that it should be less then 5% of the standard deviations. Is that in your opinion -more or less- sufficient for the estimation of reliable 95% CI as well? Also, a bit more on-topic, what would be a good rule of thumb for the effective sample size when running STAN models?

- Marcel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Auto-correlation despite long chains & simple model
parts:
I didn't know that BUGS had built in effective sample size
estimation. I'd always used it through R2WinBUGs, which uses
the R Coda package.

There are many ways to estimate effective sample size and Stan (as
implemented in our chains object and in RStan) tends to be
more conservative than other estimates in cases where there
has not been convergence.

The (square root of) n_eff goes into the denominator of the MCMC
error calculation.

How much error you can tolerate depends on your application!

Note that these n_eff values are for the mean, not for the variance
or for the 95% interval. I'm not sure how to calculate the standard
error for a 95% interval's boundary points. Hopefully someone else
can help here.

- Bob
